## Overview

This is the second part of two for practicing calculating measures of community diversity. In part 1, we explored the diversity metrics for a single community, or alpha diversity. In this part 2, we will explore the diversity metrics across mutliple communities, or beta diversity.

## 1b. Read in files and explore their contents, structure.
 
```{r read in data}
d = read.delim("kmd_test_set.txt", header=T)
rownames(d) <- d$Cluster

f = read.delim("kmd_test_second.txt", header=T)
```

For community ecology analyses, we ususall have two data matrixes: a primary matrix that is called a taxa table, and a secondary matrix of metadata. The primary matrix has one column for every sample, and one row for each taxon (or OTU, or as called in this dataset, cluster). 

In this script, the primary matrix is called 'd' and the secondary matrix is called 'f'. 


```{r generate test data}
flavors <- c("Berry Blue", "Blueberry", "Bubble Gum", "Buttered Popcorn", "Cantaloupe", "Cappuccino", "Caramel Corn", "Chocolate Pudding", "Cinnamon", "Coconut", "Cotton Candy", "A&W Cream Soda", "Crushed Pineapple", "Dr Pepper", "French Vanilla", "Green Apple", "Island Punch", "Juicy Pear", "Kiwi", "Sunkist Lemon", "Lemon Drop", "Lemon Lime", "Licorice", "Sunkist Lime",  "Mango", "Margarita", "Mixed Berry Smoothie", "Sunkist Orange", "Orange Sherbet", "Peach", "Pina Colada", "Sunkist Pink Grapefruit", "Plum", "Pomegranate", "Raspberry", "Red Apple", "A&W Root Beer", "Sizzling Cinnamon", "Sour Cherry", "Strawberry Cheesecake", "Strawberry Daquiri", "Strawberry Jam", "Sunkist Tangerine", "Toasted Marshmallow", "Top Banana", "Tutti-Fruitti", "Very Cherry", "Watermelon", "Wild Blackberry")

# Generate the matrix: 100 samples (rows) × 49 flavors (columns)
jellybean_matrix <- matrix(
  sample(10:100, size = 100 * 49, replace = TRUE),
  nrow = 100,
  ncol = 49,
  dimnames = list(paste0("Sample_", 1:49), flavors)
)

```


To make the script reproducible, we will set a variable 'X' to point to the object containing the dataset we want to analyze. Here, we will define 'community' as only the part of the dataframe that contains the taxa abundances. 

```{r}
comm <- d[,2:186]
```


Explore the data. This is a small dataset, but in microbial ecology, it is usual to have thousands to tens of thousands of taxa. These datasets are much to large to view directly, so they have to be explored. 

Think of data exploration as a set of hypotheses that you test, in an iterative progression, with each experiment including expected results and evidence for whether you can accept or reject each hypothesis. 

What kind of object is my data? What are the dimensions of my data? What are the variable names? What is the structure of my data object? 
```{r exploring data}
class(d)
dim(d)    # 1000 211
names(d)
head(d)   # Display the first six rows of the data
str(d)    # this is the matrix with taxa only
```
We are using many of the same data exploration techniques as we used in the alpha diversity section, but some are different. What are some differences and why can't we use the same methods for alpha and beta diversity?

## 2. Richness & diversity calculations

Because richness and diversity are properties of single communities, and this dataset is a collection of 185 communities (variables, or columns in 'comm'), we need to make calculations across all the rows. R is very good at matrix algebra; you may want to review this topic ...

To calculate richness, first we need to convert abundance tables to presence-absence. 

```{r}
d.pa = d[,2:186]
threshold = 1
for(x in 1:length(d.pa)){
 	d.pa[which(d.pa[,x]>=threshold),x] = 1
 	d.pa[which(d.pa[,x] < threshold),x] = 0
}
```

Let's explore this a bit to make sure it worked. 
```{r}
d.pa[1:8,1:7]
d.pa[40845:40852,1:7]
```

Why do you think there are mostly 1s for the lower-numbered clusters, and mostly zeros for the higher-numbered clusters?
>

Now we can use the presence/absence table to calculate observed richness. The adds the total for all the columns (variables, or sites), and then performes some exploratory analysis. 
```{r}
total.richness = sapply(d.pa,sum)
head(total.richness)
hist(total.richness)
summary(total.richness)
```

It looks there is an outlier sample wiht a very high total richness. We can use which() to find it. this will return the item number (not the richness value). The second line of code subsets the total.richness vector to show the value of that index in the vector. 
```{r}
which(total.richness > 5000)
total.richness[29] # 7532
d1 <- d[, -30]
f1 <- f[-29,]

d.pa1 = d1[,2:185]
threshold = 1
for(x in 1:length(d.pa1)){
 	d.pa1[which(d.pa1[,x]>=threshold),x] = 1
 	d.pa1[which(d.pa1[,x] < threshold),x] = 0
}

total.richness = sapply(d.pa1,sum)
head(total.richness)
hist(total.richness)
summary(total.richness)
```


This line adds the calculation to the secondary matrix. This is so we can use the data on the samples (variables, or sites) to peform statistics. 
```{r}
rownames(f1) <- f1$ID
f1$total.richness <- total.richness[rownames(f1)]
head(f1)
```

Now that we have observed richness calculated for all the sites, we can perform statistics on richness. In this case we want to know if richness varies by site, and if it varies by site if we separate soil samples "Soil" from litter samples "Litt".

```{r}
summary(aov(total.richness ~ site, data=f1)) # n.s.
summary(aov(total.richness ~ site, data=f1[f1$type=="Soil",])) # p = 0.0386 *
summary(aov(total.richness ~ site, data=f1[f1$type=="Litt",])) # n.s.
```

Because there was a difference in total richness by soil type, we will keep them separate and explore if there is a variation in richness over time ("T"). This treats time as a discreet variable, but in some cases it will make more sense to treat time as a continuous variable. 
```{r}
summary(aov(total.richness ~ T, data=f1[f1$type=="Soil",])) # ***
summary(aov(total.richness ~ T, data=f1[f1$type=="Litt",])) # ***
TukeyHSD(aov(total.richness ~ T, data=f1[f1$type=="Soil",]))
TukeyHSD(aov(total.richness ~ T, data=f1[f1$type=="Litt",]))
```

Now we'll make a plot of richness. This uses base R. 
```{r}
boxplot(total.richness ~ T, data=f1[f1$type=="Soil",], ylab="Richness (number of taxa)",
	boxwex=0.3, at=1:6 - 0.2, col="grey50")
boxplot(total.richness ~ T, data=f1[f1$type=="Litt",], 
	boxwex=0.3, at=1:6 + 0.2, add=TRUE)
legend(0.5,3000,c("Soil","Litter"), fill=c("grey50","white"))

```


Here is a different way to plot 
```{r}
t.test(total.richness ~ type, data=f1) # n.s.

y = tapply(f1$total.richness, f1$type, mean) # Litt 232.266, Soil 213.143
yci = tapply(f1$total.richness, f1$type, sd) # sd Litt 59.3, Soil 52.6

stripchart(total.richness ~ type, data=f1, method="jitter", vertical=TRUE, pch=21,
	ylab="Richness", xlim=c(0.5,2.5), ylim=c(0,5000))
text(1,y[1],"_________", cex=2)
text(2,y[2],"_________", cex=2)
plotCI(c(1,2), y, yci, add=TRUE, pch=NA, scol="grey10", sfrac=0.08)
text(0.7,490,"P<0.05")
```

Now we can measure the other metrics of diversity and add them to the secondary matrix. 

```{r}
divB = t(d[d$Taxonomy=="Bacteria",2:186])
H <- diversity(divB, index="shannon") # Shannon's diversity
# this can also calculate simpsons and inverse simpsons

J = H/log(specnumber(divB)) # Pielou's J evenness index
f2 = cbind(f1,H,J)

```
